questions.question: Q1. In the Calibrate & Commission tab, why does the motor stay completely still as you sweep the pulse from 1000 us to 1050 us?

answers.b: Those pulses fall inside the arming dead-band, which gates effective throttle to 0%
answers.c: The battery voltage is too low to spin the motor
answers.d: The PWM frequency is too high

explanations.a: Incorrect — calibration is intact; this is intended behaviour.
explanations.b: Correct — pulses from 1000 us up to the 1050 us dead-band edge are gated to 0% effective throttle, so the rotor stays still even though the raw map reads up to 5%.
explanations.c: Incorrect — voltage is adequate; the dead-band is the cause.
explanations.d: Incorrect — frequency does not gate the bottom of the throttle range.

questions.question: Q2. On the Expected vs Obtained chart, your amber recorded points do not lie exactly on the dashed ideal line. What is the chart demonstrating?

answers.a: The simulator is miscalculating the throttle
answers.b: A real ESC departs from the ideal linear map — an idle dead-band, plus any endpoint-calibration error or receiver jitter
answers.c: That a higher PWM frequency would add resolution
answers.d: That the battery is discharging during the sweep

explanations.a: Incorrect — the deviations are physical behaviour, not a calculation error.
explanations.b: Correct — the Expected line is the ideal straight map; the Obtained curve adds the real dead-band near idle and, under a fault, endpoint error or jitter. The gap between the two is the calibration error you quantify (RMS / worst-case).
explanations.c: Incorrect — that is the resolution/latency misconception, unrelated to this chart.
explanations.d: Incorrect — discharge is not what the curve represents.

questions.question: Q3. Selecting 'Inverted endpoints' in the Endpoint Condition control distorts the Obtained curve how — and what real failure does it model?

answers.a: The curve is unchanged; nothing happens
answers.b: The map runs backwards, so an idle 1000 us pulse reads ~100% — the motor spins to full power on power-up
answers.d: The refresh frequency drops to zero

explanations.a: Incorrect — inverting the endpoints visibly flips the curve.
explanations.b: Correct — with the endpoints stored backwards, the idle 1000 us pulse maps to full throttle, so the motor spins to maximum the instant it is powered — a dangerous, classic mis-calibration. A stored fault also blocks arming.
explanations.c: Incorrect — resolution is unaffected by endpoint inversion.

questions.question: Q4. In the Protocol & Latency tab, switching between 50 Hz and 400 Hz changes the throttle resolution how?

answers.b: Resolution stays identical (1000 steps, 0.1% each); only the latency changes

explanations.a: Incorrect — resolution does not scale with frequency.
explanations.b: Correct — both analog frequencies resolve the same 1000 microsecond steps (0.1%/step), because resolution is set by the 1 us timer tick, not the refresh rate. Only the command latency changes (20 ms to 2.5 ms).
explanations.c: Incorrect — resolution is unchanged, not reduced.
explanations.d: Incorrect — resolution remains a finite 1000 steps.

questions.question: Q5. In the Protocol & Latency tab the amber ESC-response trace trails the blue command trace. With Standard PWM 50 Hz selected, roughly how far behind does the response lag?

explanations.a: Incorrect — ~0.03 ms (26.7 us) is a DShot600 frame, not 50 Hz.
explanations.b: Incorrect — ~2.5 ms is the 400 Hz lag.
explanations.c: Correct — latency = 1/f = 1/50 = 20 ms, so the amber response visibly trails the blue command by a full 20 ms — the delay the animation is designed to make obvious.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the whole point of the demo is the visible 20 ms lag at 50 Hz.

questions.question: Q6. In the Protocol & Latency tab, why won't the stage sign off while Standard PWM 50 Hz is selected?

answers.a: 50 Hz offers too few throttle steps
answers.b: Its 20 ms latency is too slow for flight control — you must settle on a protocol under ~5 ms (400 Hz, OneShot or DShot)
answers.c: 50 Hz is not supported by the ESC
answers.d: The motor cannot physically spin at 50 Hz

explanations.a: Incorrect — 50 Hz has the same 1000 steps as 400 Hz; resolution is not the issue.
explanations.b: Correct — 50 Hz adds 20 ms of control lag, far too slow for a multirotor. The stage requires a flight-ready protocol (latency under ~5 ms), so 50 Hz is the deliberate fault you must move past by choosing 400 Hz, OneShot or DShot.
explanations.c: Incorrect — 50 Hz is a supported (legacy) protocol.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the motor runs; the issue is command latency, not rotation.

questions.question: Q7. In the Thermal Sweep tab, what conduction loss does a 30 A phase current produce in a 30 A ESC with R<sub>ESC</sub> = 0.003 Ω?

explanations.a: Incorrect — this omits the squaring of current.
explanations.b: Incorrect — this is off by a factor of three.
explanations.c: Correct — P = I^2 * R = 30^2 * 0.003 = 900 * 0.003 = 2.7 W, which crosses the 2 W heatsink threshold.
explanations.d: Incorrect — that would require R = 0.03 ohm, ten times larger.

questions.question: Q8. With 'Hot-resistance feedback' enabled in the Thermal Sweep tab, why does the displayed dissipation climb above the cold-model prediction at the same current?

answers.a: The current increases on its own
answers.b: The MOSFET's positive Rds(on) temperature coefficient raises R_ESC as the ESC heats, so I^2*R grows at constant current
answers.c: The battery voltage rises with temperature
answers.d: The PWM duty cycle increases with temperature

explanations.a: Incorrect — the current is held fixed; only the resistance changes.
explanations.b: Correct — R(T) = R25*(1 + 0.006*(T-25)); at 80 degC R is ~33% higher, so dissipation rises (e.g. 2.7 W to ~3.6 W at 30 A) even at constant current — a thermal-runaway tendency the cold model misses.
explanations.c: Incorrect — battery voltage is not the mechanism here.
explanations.d: Incorrect — duty cycle is set by throttle, not temperature.

questions.question: Q9. In the Thermal Sweep tab, fitting the clamp-on heatsink lowers the thermal resistance R<sub>th</sub>. What does that do to the current at which the junction reaches 80 °C?

answers.a: It lowers the safe threshold current
answers.b: It raises the threshold current — the ESC carries more current before crossing 80 °C, and the hotspot at a given current falls (e.g. ~93.6 °C to ~53.4 °C at 30 A)
answers.c: It has no effect on temperature
answers.d: It removes the conduction loss entirely

explanations.a: Incorrect — lower R_th means less temperature rise per watt, so the safe current goes up, not down.
explanations.b: Correct — T = T_amb + P*R_th, so roughly halving R_th roughly halves the rise; the 80 degC crossing moves to a higher current and the hotspot drops (about 93.6 degC bare to about 53.4 degC heatsinked at 30 A).
explanations.c: Incorrect — R_th directly scales the temperature rise, so the heatsink lowers temperature.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the heatsink removes heat from the package; it does not change the I^2*R loss being generated.

questions.question: Q10. The motor phase current used to compute ESC dissipation in this experiment is carried forward from which experiment?

answers.d: It is generated randomly by the simulator

explanations.a: Incorrect — the frame experiment provides structural data, not current.
explanations.b: Incorrect — the aerodynamic experiment provides drag and efficiency, not current.
explanations.c: Correct — the motor phase current (e.g. ~7.2 A at hover) comes from the Experiment 1 propulsion/motor model, creating the inter-experiment dependency.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the current is a physically derived value, not random.
